q: In the Eighth Edition, what does agile release planning typically produce?
options: The tasks for the next two weeks, in hours each
A 3-to-6-month timeline and the number of iterations
Every single user story for the product's whole life
The daily plan of each team member
explanation: Agile release planning gives a high-level summary timeline of the release (typically 3 to 6 months), based on the roadmap and vision, and determines the number of iterations or sprints.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

q: Which artifact does the product owner replan as the team delivers and new information emerges, to show the expected sequence of deliverables over time?
options: The iteration burndown
The team charter
The definition of done
The product roadmap
explanation: Product owners may produce a product roadmap showing the anticipated sequence of deliverables over time, and replan it based on what the team produces and emerging information.

q: A new manager asks the team to estimate in hours so that dates can be promised to customers. The team prefers story points. What is the strongest reason?
explanation: Story points reflect relative effort or complexity, because teams are better at comparing work items than at predicting precise durations; estimating hours is more time-consuming and less reliable in dynamic environments. A non-numerical unit also stops the estimate being read as a firm commitment.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning
options: Relative sizes are quicker and more reliable here
Story points can be compared across every team in the company
Hours are not allowed in agile approaches
Points let managers set firm delivery dates

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Agile release planning

q: In planning poker, two members show 3 and three members show 13 for the same story. What should happen next?
options: Take the average and move on
The product owner decides on the final number
The lowest and highest explain, then all re-vote
Use 13, since it is the safest estimate
explanation: When cards differ, the team discusses the outliers: the lowest and highest estimators explain their reasons, then everyone reselects until the estimates converge.

q: A new team must size 150 backlog items in one afternoon. Which technique fits best?
options: Bottom-up estimating in hours
Affinity grouping
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
explanation: When there are many items to estimate, affinity grouping places like-sized items together on a wall. It is simple and fast, and several hundred items can be estimated in a short time.

q: A manager wants to compare two teams by velocity: one averages 40 points per iteration, the other 25. What should the project manager explain?
options: The 40-point team is clearly the more productive one
The 25-point team needs more people
Velocities can be compared after about a month
Each team's points differ, so they can't be compared
explanation: Velocity is specific to each team and cannot be used to compare their efficiency. Treating story points as interchangeable across teams ignores differences in sizing scales and definitions of done.

q: A release backlog holds 180 story points. The team's last three velocities were 22, 18 and 20. How many iterations should it plan for the release?
explanation: Average velocity = (22 + 18 + 20) / 3 = 20. Iterations = 180 / 20 = 9. Velocity normalizes over several iterations, so the team plans from its average.

q: A team averages 30 points per iteration, but the next one includes a two-day company event and a public holiday. The product owner still asks for 30 points. What should the team do?
explanation: When people are unavailable, the team cannot finish as much as in the previous period. With reduced capacity, it plans only for work that meets that capacity, and discusses this openly with the product owner.
options: Commit to 30 points as usual
Commit to 40 points to catch up later
Plan only for its reduced capacity
Cancel the iteration until all return

q: In iteration planning, the stories the product owner wants add up to more than the team can complete. What happens?
options: The team works overtime so that they all fit in
Lower-priority stories go back to the backlog
The iteration is made one week longer
The scrum master assigns the extra work
explanation: If the estimates do not fit, the lower-priority features go back into the product backlog until the workload is small enough for the team to commit.

q: In a flow-based agile team, how does the daily coordination meeting usually run?
options: Each member answers three questions in turn
The manager assigns the day's tasks to everyone
The team reviews only the iteration burndown
The team walks the board from right to left
explanation: Flow-based agile focuses on throughput: the team assesses the board from right to left, asking what is needed to advance work and whether there are bottlenecks. The three questions are typical of iteration-based agile.

q: The product owner adds 40 points of new scope halfway through a release. Which chart shows this most clearly?
options: A burnup chart, as the total-scope line rises
The ideal line of the iteration burndown chart
The kanban board's WIP limits
The release's cumulative cost curve
explanation: A burnup chart tracks the total work as a line across the top and the completed work rising from zero. Added scope shows as the top line moving up.

q: At the end of day 5, how does the iteration compare with the ideal line, and what should the team do?
options: Ahead of the ideal line, so add more work now
Exactly on the ideal line; carry on as planned
Behind the ideal line; look for what is slowing work
This cannot be seen on the chart until day 10
explanation: The ideal line falls from 50 to 0 over 10 days, so it is at 25 after day 5; the team still has 33 points. An iteration burndown shows variance against the ideal so the team can act during the iteration.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Iteration burndown chart

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Iteration burndown chart

q: Which flow metric measures the time from when a customer request is made until it is delivered?
options: Cycle time
Lead time
Throughput
Queue length
explanation: Lead time runs from the request to delivery and highlights system-wide delays. Cycle time runs from when work on an item starts until it is finished.

q: Items wait longer and longer in the team's 'Review' column, although developers finish their part quickly. Which metric shows this best?
options: Velocity
Story points
Team capacity
Queue length
explanation: Queue length counts the items waiting in each workflow state. Growing queues signal bottlenecks and hidden delays; trimming them shortens lead time.

q: Why does the Agile Practice Guide prefer empirical measures, such as finished features, to percent complete?
options: Percent done can stay green until late surprises
Finished features are easier to count by hand
Percent complete is not allowed in agile
Empirical measures need no team input
explanation: Surrogate measures like percent done often do not reflect reality: a 'watermelon' project is green outside and red inside until shortly before release. Finished work gives real data for forecasts.

q: A director makes velocity a performance target for the team. What is the likely result, according to the Agile Practice Guide?
options: Better forecasts at the portfolio level
Faster delivery at the same quality
Inflated estimates or lower quality
Fewer meetings for the team
explanation: When velocity becomes a target, teams may inflate estimates, split work unnaturally or sacrifice quality. The guide no longer recommends using velocity to assess performance or set targets.

q: In a hybrid project, a regulator's audit date is a fixed milestone. How should the agile team's releases relate to it?
options: Ignore the date, since agile has no deadlines
Plan releases to deliver what the milestone needs
Convert all of the work to a critical path schedule
Ask the regulator to accept a later date
explanation: In a hybrid approach, the high-level schedule sets key milestones with predictive techniques, and adaptive streams plan their iterations inside that framework.

q: What is the main difference between a scrum board and a kanban board?
options: A scrum board shows no workflow states
A kanban board is cleared after each sprint
Only scrum boards may limit the WIP
A kanban board limits items per column
explanation: Both show workflow stages, but a kanban board sets the maximum number of items allowed in each column and keeps flowing; a scrum board is cleared after each iteration.

q: A kanban team has no iterations. How can it forecast when 50 more items will be done?
options: From its stable throughput per week
From the sponsor's preferred date
From the velocity of another team
It cannot forecast without sprints
explanation: Throughput is the count of items finished per period; stable throughput lets teams forecast with statistics and spot sudden drops.

q: How much of the backlog should be written before an agile project's work starts?
options: Every story, written and sized before work
Only the stories of the first iteration
Enough for the first release and next iteration
None, as the backlog grows only during work
explanation: There is no need to create all stories up front: only enough to understand the first release in broad brushstrokes, and then sufficient items for the next iteration.

q: Why does the scheduling standard warn against too much up-front planning in agile projects?
options: Agile teams are not allowed to plan anything
It creates a detailed but inaccurate plan
Planning belongs only to the sponsor
It removes the need for iterations
explanation: Too little up-front planning risks oversight and rework; too much increases the risk of a very detailed, inaccurate plan. The aim is enough planning to minimize duplication and rework.

q: Backlog refinement takes the team three hours every week. What may this indicate, according to the Agile Practice Guide?
options: The team is refining just about the right amount
The iterations are too short
The release plan is complete
Overpreparation, or missing skills
explanation: Teams often aim for no more than 1 hour per week of refinement. More may mean the product owner is overpreparing or the team lacks critical skills to evaluate the work.

q: A sponsor asks the agile team for an earned value report. How can story points be used?
options: PV is points planned to a date; EV is points done
EV is the hours the team has recorded so far
Story points can never be used in earned value analysis
PV is the business value of each feature
explanation: In adaptive approaches, PV is the story points planned up to a date, EV the points of stories done by then, and AC the team's cost, usually from working hours.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

q: Which unit could a team use for relative estimating, according to the estimating standard?
options: Dollars per delivered feature
Hours per task
T-shirt sizes such as S, M and L
Calendar weeks
explanation: Relative estimating uses proxies such as T-shirt sizes, often mapped to Fibonacci numbers, so the estimates are not mistaken for quantitative ones in dollars or days.

q: Why does a team keep its iterations the same length throughout the project?
options: To match the sponsor's reporting dates
To establish a cadence
To make velocity comparable across teams
To avoid having a backlog
explanation: Iterations are generally 1 to 4 weeks long, and the team keeps the duration throughout the project to establish a cadence.

q: Which TWO are flow metrics in the Agile Practice Guide?
options: Throughput
Cycle time
Story points
Planning poker
Release plan
explanation: Table 5-4 lists throughput, cycle time, lead time, work in process, escaped defects and rework, and queue length.

q: Which THREE are steps of planning poker?
options: Each member picks a card privately
All cards are revealed at the same time
The lowest and highest estimators explain
The manager sets the final value
Cards are shown one at a time in rank order
The average is always taken
explanation: Members select cards privately, reveal them together, discuss the outliers (lowest and highest explain), and re-vote until the estimates converge.

q: Which TWO statements about velocity are correct?
options: It is specific to each team
It normalizes over several iterations
It measures the business value delivered
It should be a management target
It compares teams' productivity
explanation: Velocity is the sum of relative estimates completed in an iteration, specific to the team and normalized over several iterations. It is not business value and should not be a target or a comparison.

q: Match each planning level with what it holds.
right: The expected sequence of deliverables over time
The number of iterations over 3 to 6 months
The stories and tasks of the current timebox
explanation: Figure 5-1: the vision drives the roadmap, the roadmap drives release plans, the release plan sets the iterations, and iteration plans schedule feature development.

q: Complete each statement about agile tracking.

blanks.text: Work remaining against the time left is shown by a
Time from when work on an item starts until it is finished is
The sum of story points accepted in an iteration is

explanation: A burnup shows work completed; lead time starts at the request; capacity is what the team can take on.
